The Napkin That Built a Warehouse Empire

By Priya Raman · March 14, 2025

On a spring morning in 1978, two retail executives in Los Angeles were told to clear out their desks. By the afternoon they were sitting in a coffee shop with a pen and a paper napkin, drawing the store they had always wanted to run.

The sketch showed a warehouse with steel racks reaching to the ceiling, prices well below the corner hardware store, and staff who knew how to fix a leaking pipe. It was a store for people who build things, and it would teach everyone else how to become one of them.

The opening weeks were a disaster. Almost nobody came. The founders stood by the doors and handed out dollar bills to coax shoppers inside, a stunt that cost less than a newspaper advertisement and was far more memorable.

Within a decade the company was opening a new store every week, and the orange apron had become one of the most recognisable uniforms in American retail.
